abertura: You are going to read the same argument twice. The facts are identical. One of the two was written by someone who told the listener where the argument was going; the other was not.
Mark the three statements that are true of a talk that signals its moves.

itens.t: The listener knows when the speaker is about to change direction.
It contains more information than the version without signals.
The listener can tell a concession from a conclusion.
It is longer because the speaker repeats the facts.
The listener knows, before the end, that the end is coming.
It uses more difficult vocabulary.

sec1.rationale: Signalling adds no facts and no vocabulary. It adds a map. The listener spends nothing on working out where you are, and can spend it all on what you are saying.

nota.texto: You said, in your very first lesson of this course, that what you needed was presentations in English — and discourse markers in particular. This is that, and it is the axis of the whole block, not a topic at the end of it.

abertura: Choose the better reading for each expression. You will meet all six in the second text.

itens.t: Let me start with
alts: I am opening, and this is where
this is the most important part
itens.ok: I am opening, and this is where

itens.t: Now, here is the problem
alts: I am turning; what follows is the difficulty
everything before this was wrong
itens.ok: I am turning; what follows is the difficulty

itens.t: What this means is
alts: I am repeating it more simply
I am drawing the consequence for you
itens.ok: I am drawing the consequence for you

itens.t: Having said that
alts: I am contradicting myself
I am conceding something without dropping my point
itens.ok: I am conceding something without dropping my point

itens.t: So where does that leave us
alts: I am about to close, and here is the question I will answer
I do not know the answer
itens.ok: I am about to close, and here is the question I will answer

itens.t: My recommendation is
alts: this is one option among several
this is the ask, and I am standing behind it
itens.ok: this is the ask, and I am standing behind it

nota.texto: None of them is decoration. Each one tells the listener what kind of sentence is coming — an opening, a turn, a consequence, a concession, a close, an ask. That is why removing them costs the listener so much.

abertura: Six sentences from talks. What is the speaker doing in each one?

itens.t: "Which brings me to what I am asking for."
"I want to take three minutes on where the model stands."
"None of that changes the license question."
"The team is right that the accuracy is there."
"That is the good news. The bad news is harder."
"So we would ship a product we cannot explain."

nota.titulo: Concession is the one people skip
nota.texto: Two of the six are concessions, and they are the hardest to hear as a move. Conceding is not losing the argument: it is the sentence that makes the rest of it credible, because it shows you have already considered the objection.

doc.texto: We tested the model on twelve months of data. Accuracy is ninety-four percent. The team wants to ship in October. The model cannot explain why it declines a case. Regulators in three markets now ask for that. We would have to rebuild the pipeline. Six weeks. I would hold the launch.

Let me start with where we are. We tested the model on twelve months of data, and accuracy is ninety-four percent — which is why the team wants to ship in October.

Now, here is the problem. The model cannot explain why it declines a case, and regulators in three markets now ask for exactly that. What this means is that shipping in October buys us a launch and costs us the license.

Having said that, the fix is not enormous — rebuilding the pipeline is six weeks. So where does that leave us? My recommendation is that we hold the launch until December.

abertura: Mark the three statements that are true.

itens.t: Version B contains a fact that Version A does not.
In Version B you know, before the recommendation arrives, that a recommendation is coming.
In Version A the six-week fix reads as a new problem rather than as a concession.
Version B is easier because its sentences are shorter.
Both versions end with the same ask.
Version A is more objective because it has no signposting.

sec4.rationale: Same facts, same ask, same length. What Version B adds is the reader's certainty about where each sentence sits in the argument — and that certainty is what makes an executive room follow you.

nota.texto: “Version A is more objective” feels right and is not. Signposting does not add opinion; it marks structure. Removing it does not make you neutral — it makes you hard to follow, and a room that cannot follow you decides without you.

abertura: Each opening starts a particular kind of sentence. Complete it so the move actually lands.

itens.t: Let me start with
alts: where we are today
why the team is wrong
what I am going to ask you for

itens.t: Now, here is the problem.
alts: We tested it for twelve months.
The model cannot explain its decisions.
Accuracy is ninety-four percent.
itens.ok: The model cannot explain its decisions.

itens.t: What this means is that
alts: we would launch into a market that is about to require the opposite
the pipeline was rebuilt in six weeks
the accuracy is good
itens.ok: we would launch into a market that is about to require the opposite

itens.t: Having said that,
alts: the launch date is October
I disagree with the whole approach
the fix is six weeks, not six months
itens.ok: the fix is six weeks, not six months

itens.t: So where does that leave us?
alts: I am not sure yet.
The regulators will decide.
Hold the launch, rebuild, ship in December.
itens.ok: Hold the launch, rebuild, ship in December.

nota.texto: Once you say having said that, the room is waiting for a concession — something that works against you and that you are conceding anyway. Following it with your strongest point is the most common way a signal misfires.

banco: So where does that leave us

nota.titulo: This is the skeleton of what you will say in class
nota.texto: Six sentences, and the whole argument fits in them. If you can write it, you can say it — and in class you will say it without the text in front of you.

itens.t: The accuracy figure is ninety-four percent.
The listener is told that a difficulty is coming.
The six weeks is presented as a concession, not as a new obstacle.
The recommendation is to hold the launch.
The speaker says which regulator asked for it.
The team's wish to ship in October is explained by the accuracy.

nota.titulo: Two of these are the lesson
nota.texto: The accuracy figure and the recommendation are in both — the facts never changed. And which regulator is in neither: it is the question the room will ask, and neither version answers it. That is what you close on.

itens.t: "Accuracy is ninety-four percent."
"Now, here is the problem."
"Shipping in October costs us the license."
"What this means is..."
"Rebuilding the pipeline is six weeks."
"My recommendation is that we hold."

nota.titulo: The signal is not the claim
nota.texto: A signal carries no content of its own — it tells the room what the next sentence is for. That is exactly why it can be learned separately from the argument, and why it transfers to any argument you ever have to make.
